AMLC COMMENTARY: The latest Australian Lot Feeders' Association (ALFA)/Australian Meat and Livestock Corp (AMLC) quarterly report on Australian feedlotting activity indicate a significant increase in the number of cattle placed on feed during the March 1997 quarter.

About 437,500 head of cattle were on feed at the end of March against 366,100 head at the end of December, a rise of 19.5 percent. This raised the capacity utilisation rate to 51 percent, the highest corresponding quarter since 1996.
Increased activity has been mainly confined to states outside Queensland.

Numbers on feed increased by 26,000 head in South Australia to 31,409 head at the end of March, by 16,200 head in Victoria to 29,900 head, by 14,700 head in New South Wales to 166,400, by 9,600 in Western Australia to 19,400 and by 4,900 head in Queensland to 190,400 head.
Major increases in the minor feedlotting states reflected poor pasture conditions and large supplies of plain quality cattle being offered through saleyards at low prices.

This coupled with a tightening in supplies of quality domestic trade cattle, has led to increased premiums for well finished cattle and, as a result, a window of opportunity to feed young cattle for the domestic trade.

The survey showed a large increase in the number of cattle for the domestic market. Compared with December, when 94,900 cattle in feedlots were aimed at the domestic trade (25.9 percent of total capacity), the number intended for domestic consumption has risen 54,500 head to 149,400 head (34.1 percent of the total).

In the current quarter to June, feedlot activity is expected to consolidate, rising by four percent to 455,000 head. The main increase is expected in Queensland and will be primarily dependant on conditions in the Japanese and Korean markets. Weather will also have a major influence on activity over the current quarter.
Unless an autumn break is received in the next few months, domestic feedgrain supplies will become precious and may force feedlotters to adjust inventory levels.

In export beef markets, US prices fell this week as larger supplies of beef hit the spot market. Larger supplies were a function of both increased domestic cow slaughter and higher import volumes. Domestic grinding beef prices fell by three to seven US cents per pound with the largest falls incurred in the lean sections.
Australian lean beef prices in the US market were pressured down by the fall in US domestic beef prices. Prices slipped three US cents a lb to 88USc/lb for 90CL manufacturing beef.
Over the past month returns to Australian exporters, although assisted by a falling exchange rate, have declined by around 26 Ac/kg.

In the Japanese market the news remains gloomy. Prices for most items eased slightly with the exception of striploin, tenderloins and shortfed fullsets which registered small gains. Offers for frozen product were also wound back in line with the easing U.S. market.
Traders are bemused with the lack of interest in beef in the lead-up to the Golden week holiday period. However, demand for pork remains solid even though prices continue to rise.

This suggests that consumer demand may still be affected by last year's E. Coli food poisoning outbreak which stifled demand for items that are served raw. Further evidence of this is that demand for beef items that require cooking before consumption remain reasonably steady in comparison to other items.

Unless there is a recovery in beef demand in north Asia over the next few months, with increasing supplies of US beef forecast to reach the market by the end of May, a softening in international beef prices may be around the corner.
The effect of this on the Australian industry will be magnified unless there is an autumn rain break over the next few months to slow the supply of unfinished cattle entering saleyards.
Cattle prices this week held for top quality lines but were weaker for lesser quality stock.
Although yardings were significantly reduced, prices struggled because of heavy yardings and processed levels over the past two weeks.
This, coupled with the holiday-shortened working week, meant processors did not require as many cattle as in previous weeks. The largest falls were in Queensland and South Australia.
The Queensland cattle market index fell 3.7 points during the week to 85.7 points, the lowest since mid-January this year and before that late July 1996.
Friday is the Anzac Day public holiday in Australia.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
